review:
Two men, one rock, and a light neither of them is allowed to look at. Robert Eggers shoots in black and white on a nearly square frame, and the aspect ratio does more work than any line of dialogue — the walls are always close, the sky is always cut off, and the sea arrives from somewhere just outside the picture.

Dafoe gets the monologues and deserves them. His curse upon Pattinson's cooking runs the better part of a minute and builds like weather. But Pattinson has the harder job: he has to be the audience's foothold and then lose that footing so gradually that you cannot name the scene where it happened.

The film is often called a horror, which undersells how funny it is. Two men trapped together become tedious long before they become frightening, and Eggers is unusually honest about the tedium — the farting, the bickering over whose turn it is, the terrible sameness of the meals. The madness, when it comes, feels less like possession than like boredom finally reaching its logical end.

The fog horn on the soundtrack never stops. By the final reel you will not remember when it started.
